facts.claim: The song was written by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards and produced by Andrew Watt, and it grew out of a piano composition by Jagger.
Stevie Wonder plays Fender Rhodes, Moog and piano on the track, alongside a major vocal performance by Lady Gaga.
It was recorded at Henson Recording Studios in Los Angeles, Metropolis Studios in London and Sanctuary Studios in Nassau, Bahamas.
Discogs credits Steve Jordan on drums, Keith Richards on bass, Serban Ghenea as mixer and Matt Colton as mastering engineer. Polydor Records is listed as the record company.
The band recorded the song largely live at Henson in January 2023, playing together in the same room, with overdubs added later.
Jagger said Gaga was recording in the same studio and walked in on the session. She curled up on the floor in front of him, someone handed her a mic, and she began singing oohs and ahs.

Producer Andrew Watt, who has Stevie Wonder tattooed on his finger, said that when Jagger played him an early piano version he thought the song called for a guest. Watt then invited Wonder, who had toured with the Stones in 1972.
Jagger described the song as kind of like a gospel song that also has personal things in it.
Wonder said the song needed a place of celebration, and that to him it was saying hello, not goodbye.
It was the second single from Hackney Diamonds, the band's first album of original material in 18 years and its first since Charlie Watts died. The album was released on 20 October 2023.

research.lineage: Press materials describe it as a gospel-infused Stones epic in the lineage of "You Can't Always Get What You Want" and "Shine A Light".

draft:
The hardest line in **Sweet Sounds Of Heaven** isn't a hymn. It's a refusal: "No, I'm not, not goin' to Hell / In some dusty motel." It's the bluntest thing in a song otherwise full of blessings and falling light, and it gives the whole thing its spine. Around it sit prayers for the hungry, the smell of heaven, children singing about the land they were born in. Then the narrator plants a foot and says this isn't how the story ends. The defiance and the devotion never settle their argument, and the song is better for leaving them both standing.

Mick Jagger called it kind of like a gospel song that also has personal things in it, and that's an accurate map. The gospel part is all over the surface: bread and wine, Father and Son, a congregation told to sing, shout, and stand up proud. The personal part leaks out in the middle of the communion. The narrator wants to laugh and cry in the same breath, wants to be "drenched in the rain" of someone's love, and admits to "finally, finally quenchin'" a thirst that has clearly lasted a long time. That doubled "finally" carries more relief than any of the praise.

The band plays it slow and patient, a relaxed gospel shuffle built on a steady kit with a fat snare, a simple walking bass, and electric guitar holding long chords while piano fills in underneath. The lead vocal is raspy and worn at the edges. The room sounds big and warm, with natural reverb around everything, which fits how it was made: the Stones cut it largely live at Henson in Los Angeles, playing together in one room with Steve Jordan on drums and Keith Richards on bass. When a higher voice comes in to harmonize, the prayer stops being one person's.

The people in that room explain a lot. It started as a piano piece of Jagger's, and producer Andrew Watt heard a guest in it and invited Stevie Wonder, who plays Rhodes, Moog and piano here and who toured with the band back in 1972. Lady Gaga was recording down the hall, wandered in, curled up on the floor in front of Jagger, and started singing oohs and ahs into a mic someone handed her. It's the same churchy reach as "You Can't Always Get What You Want" and "Shine A Light," and it was the band's first new music since Charlie Watts died. Wonder heard it as saying hello, not goodbye.

Then comes the line the whole song leans toward: "Let the old still believe that they're young." It's tender and stubborn at once, a blessing asked for by people who know exactly how old they are.

What sticks is that the song lets you feel two things at once, the grace of being carried and the plain refusal to go quietly, and it never asks you to pick one.
